title: Shopify GitHub Integration for Themes (2026 Guide)
summary: Shopify GitHub integration involves two workflows for theme management. You'll know which process fits your setup and how to begin connecting.
body_markdown:
## Shopify to GitHub workflow stages


Connect both accounts, add a Shopify trigger, map its fields into a GitHub action, then test and publish: that is the whole workflow, in four stages. A narrow token is already in hand, so the first stage is mostly pasting it in the right place.


In Activepieces, a Shopify trigger starts the flow and a GitHub action writes the result, which suits event-driven jobs like these well and theme file sync weakly.


The catalogue behind those two steps holds 750 integrations, counted directly from the` packages/pieces/community` directory of the MIT-licensed open source monorepo on GitHub, and roughly 60% of them were contributed by the community, so each one is a directory of source you can open and read rather than a line on a vendor's list.


When the GitHub action you want isn't listed, the HTTP request step covers it today, and a missing connector is something you can generate with AI and add privately to your own instance rather than wait on a vendor release for.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production.


### Stage 1: Connect Shopify and GitHub


Create one connection per app inside your automation tool, and name each so you can tell them apart later, such as "shopify-store-prod" and "github-orders-repo".


For Shopify, the connection needs your store's address and an access token from a custom app you create in the store admin. Give that app read access only to the data the trigger needs, such as orders.


For GitHub, paste the fine-grained token scoped to the one repository, with write access to issues or contents, whichever your action uses. If a connection dialog accepts the token but later steps fail with a permissions error, the scope is the first thing to check.


A connection can save successfully and still be too narrow for the action you pick.


### Stage 2: Add the Shopify trigger and load a test event


Add a new workflow, choose Shopify as the trigger, and pick the event that matches your goal, for example a new order or a new product. Select the Shopify connection from Stage 1. Then load sample data.


In the screenshot below, a trigger step is configured this way: the trigger event selected, the connection attached, and a sample-data section reporting that data loaded successfully.


Take from the screenshot that the trigger is only usable once it has a real sample, because the next stage's field picker is built from that sample.


If the sample is empty, create a test order or product in the store first and load again, otherwise you'll have nothing to map.


### Stage 3: Add the GitHub action and map fields


Add a GitHub step after the trigger, select your GitHub connection, and choose the action. Creating an issue is the safest first choice because it's easy to inspect and easy to delete.


Pick the repository, then map fields by inserting values from the trigger sample: order number into the title, customer-facing details and line items into the body.


Leave out anything personal that the repository doesn't need, since repo contents are often visible to more people than the store admin is.


If the action you want isn't in the connector's list, add a plain HTTP request step instead and send the call to GitHub's API with the same token in an authorization header.


### Stage 4: Test, publish and check the result


Run the test on the GitHub step, then open the repository and confirm the issue or file appeared with the right values in the right places. Fix mapping mistakes now, while only a test record exists.


Once it looks right, publish the workflow, then place one real order or product edit in the store and watch the repository again. That second check proves the live trigger fires, not just the sample.


If nothing arrives, look at the workflow's run history before changing anything, because it shows whether the trigger never fired or the GitHub step rejected the request.
